name: messaging-gateway
intent: Encapsulate access to a messaging system behind an ordinary interface of domain methods, so calling application code makes method calls while a single component owns message construction, correlation, timeouts and error translation.
problem: Application code that talks to a broker keeps importing messaging concepts: it builds the payload, picks the channel, attaches a reply address and a correlation id, parses the response and interprets broker errors. The trigger for this pattern is that callers should make a method call instead of writing messaging code - the messaging knowledge belongs in exactly one place that can change without touching business rules.
context: At the boundary between application logic and a messaging system (message broker, MQ, queue service or actor runtime): the other side is reached by messages, but the caller is ordinary domain code that should see typed parameters and typed results. Applies to one-way (fire and forget) and request-reply interactions alike, and to blocking as well as asynchronous call styles.
benefits: Application code depends only on a domain interface: no messaging types, channel names, headers or serialization in business logic.

Transport changes stay inside the gateway - swapping broker or protocol, or substituting a fake in tests, does not touch callers - which is exactly the property frameworks advertise when they promise a transporter swap without application changes.
One place owns the concentrated, error-prone part: payload assembly, correlation, timeouts, retries and fault-to-exception translation.
Typed signatures give compile-time checking, IDE discoverability and a trivial test seam: a fake implementation replaces the broker in unit tests.
Messaging policy (wire format, correlation-id propagation, error contract) is standardized once for every interaction with that system.
Later optimizations - caching, batching, asynchronous return types, a different interaction style - stay local to the gateway and invisible to callers.
tradeoffs: The method-call illusion hides a network round trip: a locally looking call can block for the whole reply timeout, so latency and partial failure must be designed for rather than discovered.

Reply handling is real state: correlation tables, reply queues or pending futures must be bounded and cleaned up, and late or duplicate replies must be discarded - a consumer that restarted after answering will answer the same request twice.
Every typed signature becomes a wire contract: changing a parameter or return type changes the message the other system must accept, so internal domain objects must not be sent as-is.

Error semantics degrade across the boundary: broker faults, timeouts and remote exceptions must be mapped to domain errors, and the mapping is lossy - the original stack trace and the distinction between 'not delivered', 'not processed' and 'answer lost' disappear.
It slides easily into a chatty remote-object interface: one gateway method per remote getter produces many round trips where one message would do.
For same-process or already-message-oriented callers it is pure indirection: a facade over code that was not the problem.
A gateway that accumulates business logic becomes a god object at the seam; it has to stay a translator.

participants.responsibility: Calls domain methods on the gateway and knows nothing about messages, channels, headers or correlation.
The domain-facing contract: one method per interaction, typed in domain terms, carrying no messaging types.
Turns a method call into send/receive operations against the messaging system and owns the lifecycle of that call.
Maps method arguments to payload and headers and back again, including correlation id and reply address, without letting the wire format leak outward.
Attaches the reply address, keeps the pending calls, matches each reply by correlation id and completes the corresponding result or failure.
Converts transport faults, timeouts and fault/error messages into domain exceptions or error results.
The underlying send/receive machinery the implementation delegates to; it stays private to the gateway.

use_cases: A domain service that must query another system (inventory, pricing, credit scoring) over a queue: the caller invokes checkStock(sku) and receives a typed answer.
An HTTP or API layer whose controller awaits a brokered round trip (Spring Integration gateway interface, NestJS ClientProxy, MassTransit request client).
Batch and background jobs that dispatch work through a typed job API instead of assembling payloads (ActiveJob perform_later, Celery delay).
Wrapping a legacy system's MQ interface once, so the rest of the codebase never learns its message format.
Test seams: unit tests substitute a fake gateway, integration tests run the same interface against a real broker.
Migration seam: keep the gateway contract stable while the transport moves from one broker to another.
Actor and streaming stacks where a facade wraps ask/request so callers never hold ActorRefs or inboxes.
Spring Integration's @MessagingGateway and GatewayProxyFactoryBean let application code inject a typed interface while the framework routes calls into channels and returns replies.
MassTransit's IRequestClient<T> and GetResponse<TResponse> provide a typed request-reply client over the bus, keeping request and response message contracts out of the calling service.
RabbitMQ's RPC tutorial demonstrates a gateway-like client that publishes to rpc_queue with reply_to and correlation_id, then resolves the matching callback response.
avoid_when: Messages are one-way events with no answer: a publisher plus an event-driven consumer is simpler, and correlation machinery is pure overhead.
Caller and callee live in one process without a messaging requirement: a plain interface call is cheaper and has no failure modes to design.
The caller is already a message consumer inside a message-oriented pipeline: use Message Endpoint or Service Activator directly instead of adding a facade over a facade.
The interaction fans out to many responders (quotes from several suppliers): use Scatter-Gather or a publish-subscribe channel; a single-reply gateway models it wrongly.
The transport is a log or stream consumed event-wise: forcing request-response onto a streaming transporter fights the model, so prefer the event style.
anti_patterns: A gateway that leaks the messaging API: methods take message objects or headers, or callers must set correlation ids and reply addresses themselves.
Chatty remote-object facade: one method per remote getter, so one screen costs dozens of round trips that a single message could carry.
Blocking gateway with no timeout or error model: calls hang when the broker is down and worker threads pile up.
Business logic inside the gateway (routing, aggregation, validation rules): the seam becomes a god object.
Retrying at the call site after a timeout without idempotency: the request may already have been executed, so the retry duplicates the effect.
A generic send(destination, anything) escape hatch: the typed contract is lost and callers are writing messaging code with extra steps.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: callers depend on a domain interface; the broker API is an implementation detail.
Single responsibility: the gateway translates calls into messages and does nothing else.
Information hiding: header names, payload formats and correlation ids never cross the boundary.
Interface segregation: publish use-case-shaped methods, not a generic send/receive pair.
Fail fast at the boundary: explicit timeouts and a small domain error set instead of hanging or leaking broker codes.
One gateway per external system, so responsibility for a failing interaction stays attributable.
best_practices: Name methods and exceptions in domain terms and keep the messaging vocabulary out of the interface.
Give every call an explicit timeout and document what it means - 'unknown outcome', not 'not executed'.
Make remote calls recognizable as remote, and return asynchronous types where the caller can handle them instead of blocking a thread.
Keep one method per message: coarse-grained operations, never a mirror of the remote object's accessors.
Own the correlation state: bound it, expire it, discard replies with unknown ids, and make remote operations idempotent because duplicates are possible.
Translate faults, broker errors and timeouts into a small domain error set at the boundary; never leak broker types or codes.
Test callers against a fake gateway and the gateway itself against a real broker, including the no-responder and timeout paths.
Keep wire DTOs in the gateway (Messaging Mapper) instead of reusing domain entities as the message contract.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Messaging Gateway (Messaging Endpoints chapter).
